steps.stem: How many three-digit numbers can be made from the digits 3, 5, 6 and 9 if the hundreds digit is smaller than the tens digit and the tens digit is smaller than the units digit?
explanation: List in order, smallest first. Hundreds digit \(3\): \(356\), \(359\), \(369\). Hundreds digit \(5\): \(569\). Hundreds digit \(6\) or \(9\): there are not enough bigger digits left.
Total: \(4\) numbers.
Check: each number uses \(3\) of the \(4\) digits, in increasing order. So we only choose the \(1\) digit that is left out: \(4\) ways.

steps.stem: A food truck offers 7 soups and 3 kinds of bread. A lunch contains one soup and one kind of bread. How many different lunches are possible?
explanation: Two stages: a soup (\(7\) options) and a bread (\(3\) options).
Multiply: \(7\times3=21\) lunches.
Adding, \(7+3=10\), counts menu items, not lunches.

steps.stem: A locker number has two digits, each from 0 to 9. The sum of the two digits must be 14. How many locker numbers are possible?
explanation: First digit: it must be at least \(5\) (otherwise the second digit would have to be more than \(9\)). So \(5, 6, 7, 8, 9\): \(5\) options.
Second digit: it must be \(14\) minus the first digit. It is forced: \(1\) option.

steps.stem: A suitcase lock has three wheels. Each wheel shows one of the digits 1 to 9, and digits may repeat. How many codes are possible?
explanation: Digits may repeat, so the pool stays the same: \(9\) options for each wheel.
\(9\times9\times9=729\). Codes like \(777\) and \(373\) are included.

steps.stem: A suitcase lock has three wheels. Each wheel shows one of the digits 1 to 9, and no digit may appear twice. How many codes are possible?
explanation: No digit may repeat, so the pool shrinks: \(9\), then \(8\), then \(7\).
\(9\times8\times7=504\).
Compare with the previous question: the same digits, but \(9\times9\times9\) became \(9\times8\times7\).
We do not divide by anything: \(123\) and \(213\) are different codes (\(\frac{504}{6}=84\) is the trap).

steps.stem: In how many different ways can 7 different trophies be placed in a row in a glass cabinet?
explanation: \(7\) trophies in a row: \(7!=7\times6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1=5040\).
The last place has only \(1\) trophy left: it is forced.

steps.stem: Six towns are connected so that every pair of towns has exactly one direct two-way bus line. How many bus lines are there?
explanation: Count in order: the line leaves from one of \(6\) towns and goes to one of the \(5\) others: \(6\times5=30\).
A line from A to B is the same line as from B to A, so every line was counted twice: \(\frac{30}{2}=15\).

steps.stem: How many diagonals does an eight-sided polygon have?
explanation: From each vertex: \(8-3=5\) diagonals (not to itself and not to its two neighbors).
Every diagonal is counted from both of its ends: \(\frac{8\times5}{2}=20\).
Or: all lines between the vertices, \(\frac{8\times7}{2}=28\), minus the \(8\) sides: \(28-8=20\).

steps.stem: A breakfast stand offers 6 hot drinks and 5 pastries. A customer chooses one of each. If the drink is espresso, the pastry must be a croissant; with any other drink, any pastry is allowed. How many choices are possible?
explanation: Case 1, espresso: the pastry must be a croissant. \(1\times1=1\).
Case 2, another drink: \(5\times5=25\).
The cases do not overlap, so add them: \(1+25=26\).
Check: all pairs, \(6\times5=30\), minus the forbidden pairs (espresso with the \(4\) other pastries): \(30-4=26\).

steps.stem: A green dice and a yellow dice each show a number from 1 to 6. How many ordered outcomes have a sum different from 8?
explanation: All outcomes: \(6\times6=36\).
All minus forbidden: \(36-5=31\).

steps.title: Counting possibilities
steps.intro: Work in stages: how many options at each stage — then decide whether to multiply, add, subtract or divide.

tables.title: The 5-step checklist
head: Step
Ask
Then
rows: a row or a code: yes · a group: no (divide by \(k!\))
yes: the pool stays full · no: the pool shrinks
most restricted position first; a forced position \(=1\)
divide by \(2\) (mutual action) or by \(k!\) (a group)
separate cases: add · "not", "at least one": all \(-\) forbidden

tables.title: Which rule?
head: Situation
Count
Example
rows: multiply the options at each stage
Later choice depends on an earlier one
imagine the first pick, then count what is really left
the pool shrinks by one each stage
count as usual, then divide by \(2\)
A group, order does not matter
Groups with no names (pairs, unnamed teams)
count as if the groups had names, then \(\div\) (number of groups)\(!\) · pairs: fix one person, choose her partner
4 girls into 2 pairs: \(\frac{6}{2!}=3\) (not \(6\)) · 6 players into 3 pairs: \(5\cdot3\cdot1=15\)

tips: First decide what makes two results different: a row or a code cares about order — a group does not.
Dividing by \(2\) or by \(k!\) needs a reason: the same object was counted more than once.
Not sure about a formula? Test it on a small case you can draw: 4 people, \(\frac{4\times3}{2}=6\) handshakes.
Choices that differ by a factor (\(210\) and \(35\))? Order matters: the bigger one. A group: divide.

steps.stem: In how many different ways can a team of 11 players be chosen from a squad of 12 players?
explanation: Choosing \(11\) of \(12\) is the same as choosing the \(1\) player who stays out: \(12\) ways.
The long way gives the same: \(\frac{12\times11\times10\times\cdots\times2}{11!}=12\).

steps.stem: Ten hikers are split between two guides, Lena and Omar, with five hikers assigned to each guide. How many different splits are possible?
explanation: Choose Lena's \(5\) hikers as if order mattered: \(10\times9\times8\times7\times6\).
The order inside the group does not matter, so divide by \(5!=5\times4\times3\times2\times1\).
Cancel: \(\frac{10\times9\times8\times7\times6}{5\times4\times3\times2\times1}=3\times2\times7\times6=252\) (\(10\) cancels with \(5\times2\), \(9\div3=3\) and \(8\div4=2\)).
The other \(5\) hikers go to Omar: \(1\) option. The guides have names, so we do not divide by \(2\) again (\(126\) is that trap).

steps.stem: What is the ratio of the number of row arrangements of 9 distinct objects to the number of row arrangements of 7 distinct objects?
explanation: The ratio is \(\frac{9!}{7!}=\frac{9\times8\times7!}{7!}=9\times8=72\).
There is no need to calculate \(9!=362{,}880\) and \(7!=5040\) first.
Take out the smaller factorial: \(10!=10\cdot9!\), so \(10!-9!=9!\cdot(10-1)=9\cdot9!\).
Or write both in terms of \(8!\): \(10!=90\cdot8!\) and \(9!=9\cdot8!\). So \(\frac{90\cdot8!-9\cdot8!}{8!}=90-9=81\).
The traps: \(90=\frac{10!}{8!}\) forgets the \(-9!\). \(\frac{1}{8!}\) comes from the wrong rule \(10!-9!=(10-9)!\).

steps.stem: How many three-digit numbers have a hundreds digit and a units digit whose sum is 8?
explanation: Most restricted position first: the hundreds digit. It is not \(0\) and not more than \(8\): \(1\) to \(8\), so \(8\) options.
Units digit: forced (\(8\) minus the hundreds digit): \(1\) option.
Tens digit: free, \(0\) to \(9\): \(10\) options.
\(8\times10\times1=80\).

Check: the (hundreds, units) pairs are \((1,7)\), \((2,6)\), \((3,5)\), \((4,4)\), \((5,3)\), \((6,2)\), \((7,1)\), \((8,0)\). That is \(8\) pairs, each with \(10\) possible middle digits. (\(90\) wrongly lets the number start with \(0\).)

steps.stem: In a table-tennis league, each pair of players plays exactly one match. There are 66 matches altogether. How many players take part?
explanation: With \(n\) players, each pair plays once: \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=66\).
Multiply by \(2\): \(n(n-1)=132\). Two consecutive numbers with product \(132\): \(12\times11\). Therefore \(n=12\).
Check the other choices: \(\frac{13\times12}{2}=78\), \(\frac{11\times10}{2}=55\), \(\frac{9\times8}{2}=36\).

steps.stem: Eight children all have different heights. A photographer chooses seven of them and places them in a row from shortest to tallest. How many different rows can be formed?
explanation: Choose the \(1\) child who stays out: \(8\) options.
The other \(7\) stand from shortest to tallest: only \(1\) order.
\(8\times1=8\). We do not multiply by \(7!\): the height order is forced.

steps.stem:
The digits 2, 5, 6 and 9 go once each into a square: A and B on top, C and D below.
A is even.
\(C\times D\) is even.
How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Most restricted first. A is even: \(2\) or \(6\), so \(2\) options.
\(C\times D\) is even only if C or D is even. The only other even digit must go to the bottom row, so B must be odd: \(5\) or \(9\), so \(2\) options.
The last two digits go into C and D in \(2\times1=2\) orders.
\(2\times2\times2\times1=8\).
Check: with A even there are \(2\times3!=12\) arrangements. The bad ones have the other even digit in B: \(2\times1\times2=4\). \(12-4=8\).

steps.stem: A code has 4 digits. Each digit is from 0 to 9, digits may repeat, and the code may start with 0. How many codes contain the digit 5 at least once?
explanation: At least one \(=\) all \(-\) none.
Codes with no 5: each digit has \(9\) options: \(9^4=6561\).

steps.stem: Five different letters are put into 3 mailboxes. A mailbox may get any number of letters, or none. In how many different ways can the letters be put into the mailboxes?
explanation: Each letter chooses a mailbox: \(3\) options for each of the \(5\) letters.
\(3\times3\times3\times3\times3=3^5=243\).
The trap \(5^3=125\) lets each mailbox choose one letter, but a mailbox may get several letters, or none.

steps.stem: Six different books are placed on a shelf in a row. The 3 math books among them must stand together, in any order. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Glue the \(3\) math books into one block. Now there are \(4\) items: the block and the \(3\) other books. \(4!=24\) orders.
Inside the block, the math books can stand in \(3!=6\) orders.

steps.stem: Three boys and two girls stand in a row. All five are different people. The two girls may not stand next to each other. How many orders are possible?
explanation: Gaps: first place the boys: \(3!=6\) orders. They make \(4\) gaps: before, between and after them.
Each girl goes into a different gap: \(4\times3=12\).
Check with all minus together: all orders \(5!=120\). Girls together (glue): \(4!\times2=48\). \(120-48=72\).

steps.stem: How many different arrangements of all the letters of the word BANANA are there? (An arrangement does not have to be a real word.)
explanation: If all \(6\) letters were different: \(6!=720\).
A appears \(3\) times: swapping the As gives nothing new, so divide by \(3!=6\). N appears \(2\) times: divide by \(2!=2\).

steps.stem: Six people sit around a round table. Two arrangements are the same if one is a rotation of the other. Dana and Eli must sit next to each other. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Glue Dana and Eli into one block. Now there are \(5\) items around the table.
Round table: fix one item and arrange the others: \((5-1)!=4!=24\).
Inside the block: \(2\) orders (Dana on the left or on the right of Eli). \(24\times2=48\).
Check: fix Dana's seat. Eli sits in one of the \(2\) seats next to her, and the other \(4\) people fill the other seats in \(4!=24\) ways: \(2\times24=48\).

steps.title: Advanced counting tools
steps.intro: The shortcuts from the advanced counting questions and the two method videos.

head: Tool
Rule
Example
rows: break every factor into primes, count each prime
once an earlier choice decides it: 1 option

tables.title: More methods
head: Situation
Method
Example
rows: glue into one block, \(\times\) the order inside
place the others, then fill the gaps
divide by the factorial of each repeat

tips: A square or grid counts the same as a row: options at each stage, multiplied.
Leading digit is never 0; a middle digit can be.

steps.stem: Six different awards are given to six volunteers, one award per volunteer. In how many different ways can this be done?
explanation: The first award has \(6\) possible volunteers. \(5\) remain for the next award, then \(4\), \(3\), \(2\) and \(1\).
The product is \(6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1=720\).

steps.stem: A signal is made of 3 flags in a row. Each flag is one of 7 colors, and colors may repeat. How many signals are possible?
explanation: Colors may repeat: \(7\times7\times7=343\).

steps.stem: A group of \(n\) different dancers can line up in 24 different orders. What is \(n\)?
explanation: \(n\) dancers in a row: \(n!\) orders.
\(4!=4\times3\times2\times1=24\), so \(n=4\).

steps.stem: A gym gives each locker a different code made from the letters A, B, C, D and E, using each letter exactly once. At most how many lockers can receive a code?
explanation: The first position has \(5\) options, then \(4\) remain, then \(3\), \(2\) and \(1\).
Multiply: \(5\times4\times3\times2\times1=120\).

steps.stem: Seven chess clubs hold a league. Each club plays every other club once. How many games are played?
explanation: Each of the \(7\) clubs has \(6\) opponents: \(7\times6=42\).
Every game was counted twice (once from each club): \(\frac{42}{2}=21\).

steps.stem: A sports kit has a cap, a jersey and socks. Each item comes in 5 colors. A player chooses one of each, with all three items in different colors. How many kits are possible?
explanation: Cap: \(5\) colors. Jersey: a different color, \(4\) options. Socks: \(3\) colors left.
\(5\times4\times3=60\).

steps.stem: Six cyclists finish a race with no ties. How many different ordered podiums of first, second and third place are possible?
explanation: First place: \(6\) options, second: \(5\), third: \(4\). \(6\times5\times4=120\).
The order of the other three cyclists does not matter.

steps.stem: How many three-digit even numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 if no digit may repeat?
explanation: Most restricted first: the units digit must be even, \(2\) or \(4\): \(2\) options.
Hundreds digit: \(4\) digits left. Tens digit: \(3\) left.
\(2\times4\times3=24\).

steps.stem: Five singers must stand in the left part of a row, and three drummers in the right part. Everyone is different. How many orders are possible?
explanation: Singers in the left part: \(5!=120\) orders. Drummers in the right part: \(3!=6\) orders.
The parts cannot change sides, so \(120\times6=720\).

steps.stem: A ticket code is one of 4 letters, followed by 3 different digits chosen from 1 to 8, in order. How many ticket codes are possible?
explanation: Letter: \(4\) options. Three different digits in order: \(8\times7\times6=336\).

steps.stem: A lunch is either a main course, a side dish and a drink, or a soup and a drink. There are 4 main courses, 3 side dishes, 3 soups and 2 drinks. How many different lunches are possible?
explanation: Two separate cases. Main-course lunches: \(4\times3\times2=24\). Soup lunches: \(3\times2=6\).

steps.stem: A florist has 5 kinds of white flower and 4 kinds of yellow flower. A bouquet uses two different kinds of the same color. How many bouquets are possible?
explanation: Two white kinds: \(\frac{5\times4}{2}=10\). Two yellow kinds: \(\frac{4\times3}{2}=6\).
A bouquet is white or yellow (two separate cases), so add: \(10+6=16\).

steps.stem: At a reunion, every two guests shake hands once. There are 36 handshakes. How many guests are there?
explanation: With \(n\) guests: \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=36\), so \(n(n-1)=72=9\times8\). Therefore \(n=9\).
Check the other choices: \(8\) guests give \(28\), \(10\) give \(45\), \(18\) give \(153\).

steps.stem: Each of 4 students chooses one of 3 after-school clubs. In how many different ways can the students choose?
explanation: Each student chooses: \(3\) options for each of the \(4\) students.
\(3\times3\times3\times3=3^4=81\). (\(4^3=64\) is the trap: the clubs do not choose the students.)

steps.stem: A light signal has \(x\) lamps in a row. Each lamp shows one of 4 colors, and colors may repeat. The number of possible signals is \(2^{6n}\). What is \(x\)?
explanation: Each lamp has \(4\) options, so there are \(4^x\) signals.

Method 2 · Plugging in numbers: one equation with two letters, and the question expects one answer, therefore any values that fit give it. Take \(n=1\): \(4^x=2^6=64\), therefore \(x=3\). Only \(3n\) gives \(3\) (the others give \(6\), \(2\) and \(5\)).

steps.stem: What is the prime-factor form of \(3!\times4!\times5!\)?
explanation: Add the exponents of each prime: \(2^{1+3+3}\times3^{1+1+1}\times5=2^7\times3^3\times5\).
Know them by sight: \(720=6!\) and \(5040=7!=7\cdot6!\).
The trap \(7\) forgets the \(1\) (the \(6!\) itself).

steps.stem:
\(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers, and \(x>y\).
Given: \(\frac{x!}{y!}=110\).
Which of the following could be the value of \(x+y\)?
explanation: \(\frac{x!}{y!}\) is a run of neighbors, from \(y+1\) up to \(x\).
\(110=10\cdot11\): the run is \(10\), \(11\). It starts right after \(y\), so \(y=9\), and it ends at \(x=11\). \(x+y=20\).
Check: \(\frac{11!}{9!}=11\cdot10=110\) ✓. (A run of one number also works: \(x=110\) and \(y=109\), but \(219\) is not among the choices.)
The trap \(21\) takes \(y=10\). The run starts AFTER \(y\).

steps.stem: A six-digit code begins with 3. Each following digit is strictly larger than the previous one. How many codes are possible?
explanation: The \(5\) digits after the 3 must be bigger than \(3\) and all different: they come from \(4\), \(5\), \(6\), \(7\), \(8\), \(9\). Once they are chosen, the increasing order is forced.
Choosing \(5\) of \(6\) is the same as choosing the \(1\) digit that stays out: \(6\) ways.

steps.stem: A four-digit door code uses no zero. Its first and last digits are equal, and its third digit is three times its second. How many codes are possible?
explanation: First digit: \(9\) options. It forces the last digit: \(1\) option.
Second digit: \(1\), \(2\) or \(3\) (three times it must still be a digit from \(1\) to \(9\)): \(3\) options. It forces the third digit: \(1\) option.
\(9\times3\times1\times1=27\).

steps.stem: Five different books are arranged on a shelf. Two named books must stay together, in either order. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Glue the two named books into one block. Now there are \(4\) items: \(4!=24\) orders.
Inside the block there are \(2\) orders: \(24\times2=48\).

steps.stem: Six different books are placed on a shelf in a row. Two particular books may not stand next to each other. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Not together \(=\) all \(-\) together.
All: \(6!=720\). Together (glue the two books): \(5!\times2=240\).

steps.stem: How many different five-digit numbers can be formed using all of the digits 1, 1, 2, 2, 2?
explanation: If all \(5\) digits were different: \(5!=120\).
The digit 1 repeats \(2\) times and the digit 2 repeats \(3\) times: \(\frac{120}{2!\times3!}=\frac{120}{12}=10\).

steps.stem: Seven different keys each open exactly one of seven lockers in a gym. The matches are unknown. Using information from failed tests and putting each used key aside, at most how many key tests are needed to open every locker, counting each successful opening as a test?
explanation: The first locker may need \(7\) tests before it opens.
Then \(6\) unmatched keys remain for the next locker, then \(5\), \(4\), \(3\), \(2\) and \(1\).
"At most" → this is the Topic 21 min/max method, not a counting formula. Worst luck: every locker opens only with the last key still possible: \(7+6+5+4+3+2+1=28\) tests.

steps.stem: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women. How many committees include at least one woman?
explanation: At least one \(=\) all \(-\) none.
All committees: \(\frac{9\times8\times7}{3!}=\frac{504}{6}=84\).
No women (only men): \(\frac{5\times4\times3}{3!}=10\).

steps.stem: Eight people sit around a round table. Arrangements differing only by rotation count as the same; clockwise and counterclockwise orders count as different. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Fix one person's seat (turning everyone gives the same arrangement).
The other \(7\) sit around them in order: \(7!=5040\).

steps.stem: A coach splits 8 runners into 4 pairs for training. The pairs have no names and no order. In how many different ways can the coach split the runners?
explanation: Fix one runner and choose her partner: \(7\) options. Take the next runner without a partner: \(5\) options. Then \(3\), then \(1\).
\(7\times5\times3\times1=105\).

Check: with names (pair 1, pair 2, pair 3, pair 4): \(\frac{8\times7}{2}\times\frac{6\times5}{2}\times\frac{4\times3}{2}\times1=28\times15\times6=2{,}520\). The pairs have no names, so divide by \(4!=24\): \(\frac{2{,}520}{24}=105\).
Traps: \(2{,}520\) treats the pairs as named; \(28\) counts only one pair.

steps.stem: Five identical white beads and six different colored beads are strung in a row. No two colored beads may be next to each other. How many arrangements are possible?
explanation: Gaps: place the \(5\) white beads first. They make \(6\) gaps: before, between and after them.
No two colored beads may touch, so each colored bead needs its own gap. \(6\) colored beads and \(6\) gaps: every gap gets one colored bead.
The white beads are identical, so the only freedom is the order of the colored beads: \(6!=720\).

steps.stem: Two ordinary dice are tossed, and you are told only the sum of the two results. For how many of the possible sums can you know exactly which two numbers came up (in any order)?
explanation: Every sum from \(4\) to \(10\) can be made in at least two ways, for example \(4=1+3=2+2\) and \(10=4+6=5+5\).
So there are \(4\) such sums.

steps.stem: A six-digit code uses exactly two different digits, and each of them appears three times. The code may start with 0. The sum of its digits must be divisible by 12. How many different pairs of digits can be used? (The order of the two digits does not matter.)
explanation: If the digits are \(a\) and \(b\), the sum is \(3a+3b=3(a+b)\). It is divisible by \(12\) only if \(a+b\) is divisible by \(4\).
\(a+b=4\): \(0\) and \(4\), \(1\) and \(3\) (\(2\) pairs; \(2\) and \(2\) are not two different digits).
